title: LRM: Large Reconstruction Model for Single Image to 3D
layout_note: Three horizontal rows read as a Z: top row runs left to right (input image -> conv -> image encoder block); a curved arrow drops the image features into the middle row (positional embeddings -> decoder block -> triplane tokens -> deconv -> reshape); a vertical arrow from the right end drops into the bottom row, which runs right to left (triplane -> point features -> MLP -> scene cube -> rendered image).
grouping: Each sub-network is a dashed rounded container with its name and layer count written beside it (image encoder, image-to-triplane decoder, neural radiance field). Inside, layer types are colour coded: yellow self-attention, blue cross-attention, grey MLP, green conv; orange diamonds mark camera modulation and are keyed with the residual '+' circle in a top-right legend.
shapes_depth: Rounded rectangles with soft pastel fills and thin outlines; residual adds are small circles with '+', joined by orthogonal skip lines over each block. Token sequences are tall thin vertical cell stacks drawn as slightly 3-D slabs (green image features, white positional embeddings, teal triplane tokens). The triplane is three intersecting light-teal planes in perspective with a point projected onto each; point features are a small yellow 3-D stack. The scene is the object render inside a thin gold wireframe cube. Input and output images are framed photo squares at the left ends of the top and bottom rows. Every data item carries a 'Dim:' line giving its tensor size.
proposed_highlight: No single block is marked new; the 3-D representation is the only drawn 3-D object (the intersecting planes), placed at the turn of the Z, and the camera input is an orange cuboid whose arrows fan out to every modulation diamond.
lesson: Fold a long encoder-decoder-renderer into three rows that read as a Z, put the drawn 3-D representation (intersecting feature planes) at the bottom-right turn, and write a 'Dim:' line under every data item so tensor sizes can be followed.
notes: venue ICLR from Semantic Scholar (venue_source: semantic-scholar); year = arXiv preprint year (2311.04400). The input image and render are embedded rasters.

measured.source: computed: paperfig kb measure (non-white pixels of a <= 800 px thumbnail, white = min(R,G,B) >= 245, minus the embedded images recorded by `refs crop` (images_px; their share is photo_share, null without a record); chromatic (RGB spread > 20) and neutral pixels clustered separately by PIL median-cut + k-means (k=8 / 3); clusters within dE00 4 merged; kept if >= 0.02 of chromatic pixels / neutral ones if >= 0.03 of all non-white pixels; share = fraction of the non-photo non-white pixels)

insights.structure: Three dashed containers in a Z-shaped path: Image encoder (top row), Image-to-Triplane Decoder (middle row), Neural Radiance Field (bottom row), each annotated with layer counts and dimensions.
insights.data: Input and output are real renders of a toy giraffe, tokens are tall coloured column stacks (green image features, white positional embeddings, blue triplane tokens), the triplane is three intersecting blue planes and the NeRF is a wireframe cube around the 3-D model.
insights.emphasis: Every tensor carries an explicit 'Dim:' annotation and camera modulation is an orange M diamond explained in a top-right legend, so precise shapes rather than colour emphasize the design.
insights.flow: Top row left-to-right, a curved line drops image features into the decoder's Cross block, middle row runs right to DeConv and Reshape, then down to the triplane and the bottom row runs right-to-left to the rendered image.
insights.avoid: Dense dimension text in small font under nearly every element clutters the figure; the reversed right-to-left bottom row can surprise the reader.

arrangement.units: three dashed rounded boxes (encoder, triplane decoder, NeRF) arranged as stacked rows in a Z path
arrangement.inputs_as: real photo of the object with size annotation
arrangement.shared: camera features feed the M modulation diamonds across the decoder
